courses: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Interdisciplinary study of contemporary societal challenges through the intersecting cultural domains of art, science/technology, media and politics
Historical development of Western culture and thought from antiquity to the twenty-first century, tracing the deep historical roots of present-day societal problems
Philosophical, ethical and conceptual analysis of the ideas, norms and values shaping Western culture, and the social and ethical implications of cultural change
Critical, interdisciplinary humanities-and-qualitative-social-science analysis of cultural texts, artefacts, practices, discourses and institutions
Qualitative research methods -- ethnography, discourse analysis, (historical) document analysis and conceptual analysis -- applied to cultural phenomena
Literary and artistic analysis of texts, artworks and cultural representations
Academic writing, structured argumentation and public debate about contemporary cultural and social questions
Independent scholarly research on a self-chosen arts-and-culture topic, culminating in the Bachelor thesis
adjacent: Marginalised voices and cultural representation: how the voices and experiences of marginalised groups are represented or excluded in history, public debate and literature
Technology, ethics and the arts: the ethical issues raised by emerging technologies and how art and literature help explore them
Democracy, citizenship and public culture: what it does and could mean to be a democratic society today
Culture and climate change: how scientists, states, activists and industry understand and respond to climate change on a global scale
Bodies, identity and social norms: how social norms about the body are constructed, challenged or transformed
questions: Illustrative or temporary applied formats used to communicate cultural research and analysis (producing a podcast, curating an arts festival, writing a cultural-policy brief)

Graduate career and further-study trajectories the programme prepares students for (cultural policy and arts administration, museum and heritage careers, journalism/media/communication careers, education and cultural research)

trace: Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers. Contribution: Partial foundational Western philosophical relationship; UCR broad survey does not reproduce the integrated Maastricht humanities problem/course.

Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism. Contribution: Partial modern historical context for ideology/modernity; not the full integrated cultural analysis module.

Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Provides a chronological overview of warfare in the Western world from antiquity to the present. Covers weapons, technology, strategy, defence, mercenaries, cavalry, chivalry, Blitzkrieg, guerrilla warfare and nuclear arsenals, illustrating competition for mastery in Western history. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Explores philosophical foundations and implications of AI. Examines the history of AI, ethical issues like interpretability, bias and alignment, debates about AI consciousness and implications for human nature. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed. Technical computation/mathematics does not supply cultural interpretation or ethnography.

Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed. Technical computation/mathematics does not supply cultural interpretation or ethnography.

Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed. Technical computation/mathematics does not supply cultural interpretation or ethnography.

Explores theory and practice of neural networks. Students build basic networks and progress to complex networks for computer vision, and discuss recent developments in large language and image generation models. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed. Technical computation/mathematics does not supply cultural interpretation or ethnography.

Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed. Technical computation/mathematics does not supply cultural interpretation or ethnography.

Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed. Technical computation/mathematics does not supply cultural interpretation or ethnography.

This course examines how organizations are structured and evolve over time. It explores how organizational design relates to strategy, external environment, human behavior, culture, governance and performance. A particular emphasis is put on discussing the concept and enabling capabilities of organizational agility required to navigate a fast-paced world and tackle increased uncertainty. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed. Actual organizational design/agility, not an AI-governance/cultural-theory syllabus.

Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Examines historical and modern work on the philosophy of mind. Discusses Descartes’ dualism, the nature of consciousness, AI and animal minds, personal identity, transformative experiences and the influence of technology on experience. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Investigates concepts of free will, the role of luck and openness of the future. Explores relations between free will, time and the self across multiple modules and contemporary debates. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes, typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes hands‑on experiments; no technical background required. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Explores how media shape attitudes and provide answers through examples from TV and TikTok. Examines messages that teach fear, pity, admiration and allyship. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Introduces development of the documentary form. Students write a theoretical paper and produce a short documentary film, fostering understanding of documentary diversity and providing analytical tools for documentary study. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

This course introduces students to Native American history and life from the 19th through the 21st century.  It argues that power, fear, misogyny, education, genocide, and resilience shape the Indigenous past and present. Topics we explore include the “Stolen Lives” of Indian children forcibly taken from their homes and placed in Indian Boarding Schools from the 1830’s through the 1990’s; Murdered and Missing Indigenous Women and Girls in the twenty-first century; and the individual and community forms of cultural resistance and environmental regeneration that connect past with present and future generations. We learn from the Native American scholars and 2Spirit youth that speak to and with the class. Exchange of cultural and intellectual knowledge also happens when we work with Lakota students to address contemporary challenges. Legislation, memoir, novels, and Indigenous children’s stories are central to our studies. So are the analyses of contemporary music and artistic expressions and exhibitions, as well as Hollywood and Indigenous film featuring Native American histories and lives. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Provides an introduction to Western art history, tracing major artistic movements from the late Middle Ages to the present. Through close study of key paintings and their makers, students gain insight into evolving styles, techniques and cultural influences. Contribution: Partial art-history and modernity relationship; UCR chronological Western painting survey is broader in period and different in method integration.

Examines debates on modern art through various themes. Focuses on the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions, exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies. Contribution: Partial art/museum interpretation; not a separately assessed Maastricht arts-methods skill.

Explores the archaeology of community and democracy in early-democratic Greece, seeking ancient lessons on community decision-making. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Explores ancient craft production from around the world. Examines how making objects shaped human development and how ancient solutions can inform modern sustainability. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking. Contribution: Partial academic/rhetorical writing and argument construction; not the whole research-writing trajectory.

Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed. Actual primary-school oral-rhetoric pedagogy, not advanced academic research writing.

Introduces what literature is, why we read it and how to interpret it. Covers fiction, poetry, drama, non‑fiction and film narration, exploring various literary forms and genres such as graphic narratives and romance novels. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Examines autobiographical and travel writing. Explores how individuals write about self, identity and bodily experience; discusses tropes and models used to represent human experience; and considers memory and imagination in writing. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Studies complex links between literary and film narratives. Analyzes formal aspects of both media, discusses adaptation, intertextuality, viewer participation and narrative dynamics, and allows students to research topics like literature‑to‑film adaptation and cross‑cultural themes. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Explores meaning-making through creative expression. Students study and practice poetic forms, experiment with sonic poetry, performance and other unconventional forms of communication, engage with theoretical texts and produce their own creative work. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Introduces film and media as systems of meaning and cultural production. Examines how images, narratives and technologies shape perception, identity and power; covers film storytelling, representation and genres; and develops critical engagement skills. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Introduces political philosophy. Examines concepts such as authority, freedom, equality, democracy, human rights, pluralism, multiculturalism, poverty and environmental issues through classical and contemporary texts. Emphasises essay writing and presentations. Contribution: Partial democracy/authority/equality philosophical analysis; not the whole integrated Power and Democracy course.

Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Introduces rules, institutions and politics of public international law. Covers treaties, the UN, armed conflict, war crimes, refugee protection and climate change. Students analyse cases, debate issues and produce a podcast connecting law to global challenges. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Introduces EU politics. Outlines actors, institutions and decision‑making rules; examines responses to crises; and employs various approaches to study EU politics and policy‑making. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Introduces Peace & Conflict Studies. Examines definitions of peace and conflict; analyzes conflict causation, violence typologies and radicalisation; applies reconciliation and conflict‑transformation models to real‑world scenarios through lectures and portfolio work. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research. Contribution: Partial qualitative research design, meaning and small-group enquiry; not Maastricht integrated finalresearch/proposal/thesis sequence.

Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper. Contribution: Partial primary-source research/question-formulation contribution through actual1809Walcheren case; not Maastricht broad proposal module. Actual full profile focuses on1809Walcheren primary sources.

Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Builds on Sustainability Essentials I. Applies tools and knowledge to a real‑world sustainability case study and allows students to delve deeper into aspects connected to their field of interest. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. We are looking for collaborations with local companies and other institutions. The research questions are supplied by a regional institution or company that is active in areas related to sustainability in the broadest sense. In this way it is guaranteed that the research projects are indeed relevant for the Zeeland delta. Furthermore, students will have access to expertise and/or facilities of the external partner, which will broaden their perspective. Usually, there will be one person affiliated with the external partner organization involved with a project team as external advisor Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Explores sustainable water management in delta regions. Focuses on adaptation to rising seas, floods and land subsidence; engages students in projects in Zeeland; and highlights nature‑based solutions and resilient infrastructure. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Investigates natural waters and their interactions with rocks, soils and minerals. Examines biogeochemical processes and cycles, including weathering, mineral formation, absorption, water treatment and resource recovery; utilises geochemical modelling and a case study. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed. Actual geochemical modelling, soil/mineral/water processes, not discourse or cultural analysis.

Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Examines representation of environmental concerns through visual culture. Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate. Contribution: A related disciplinary contribution, with a different object, method and assessment; no whole Maastricht module or professional qualification equivalence claimed.

notes.text: These qualified responses retain genuine cultural, historical, philosophical, literary and media analysis. Technical computing, organizational study and environmental science are companion subjects, not substitutes for cultural theory. Maastricht’s ethnography, discourse and conceptual-analysis progression and 16 EC thesis remain different.

Maastricht combines content courses with separately credited skills and a scaffolded proposal/thesis sequence. UCR distributes related work across whole courses; optional independent research is additional to the scheduled 180 EC. Neither its different format nor thematic similarity establishes degree or professional equivalence.

audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht Arts and Culture studies contemporary cultural and societal questions through history, philosophy, art, literature and qualitative social research. It connects art, science and technology, media and politics through content courses, paired skills and an individual thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: Three qualified UCR alternatives approach cultural history and the arts, digital culture and ethics, or environmental culture and governance. Each has substantive related study and different companion subjects. Maastricht’s integrated methods and research sequence remain distinct.

curriculum.limitation: This 180 EC illustration selects Othering Europe, Power and Democracy, Analysing Arts II and Doing Conceptual Analysis II from restricted menus. Open 30 EC occurs in Year 3, semester 5. Progression, attendance and elective approvals apply; English research and writing lead to an English proposal and thesis.
